No published result fine-tunes a crystal foundation model to generate battery materials conditioned on a transport property like ionic conductivity. **Hypothesis.** Conditioning MatterGen's adapter on predicted ionic conductivity gives low-barrier candidates at higher hit rate than screening; transport labels are scarce but learnable. **Restructuring.** The fine-tune, generate, screen, validate loop, ~3 rounds; each diffusion sample's ~1,000 sequential denoising timesteps. None: the loop's costly steps (generating, screening, NEB-validating thousands of candidates) are embarrassingly parallel; the plan splits each across GPUs, no reordering. **If compute is the lever.** Scaling candidates to 100,000 makes the conditioned generator's hit-rate advantage over both baselines significant; at 1,000 it is within noise. **If not.** Scaling candidates does not separate conditioned from baseline hit rates; the gap stays within seed noise at every level, so fine-tuning adds nothing. **Test.** Fine-tune the adapter of the open-source MatterGen crystal model on predicted log conductivity; generate and screen 1k-100k candidates in each arm; NEB-validate the top ten; compare hit rate against unconditioned generation and screening of the ICSD database (about $576). *Compute axis.* Generated candidate crystal structures screened per arm: 1,000–100,000 candidates, 3 levels. Closest prior: not on this axis. **Check first.** Reproduce MatterGen's 38.57% S.U.N. and 0.021 Angstrom RMSD on 1,024 samples; reproduce the npj predictor's 0.85 log10 sigma MAE. Tolerance: S.U.N. within +/-3 percentage points; RMSD <= 0.1 Angstrom; predictor MAE within +/-0.1 log10 sigma.. **Would not show.** Shows predicted-conductivity and migration-barrier rankings, not measured sigma; Li conductors only; no synthesis, cycle-life, or interface data. *Cost.* Plans $575.76 of the $1,000 budget over 174 machine-hours, leaving $424.24.
